brief.notification_title: Quiet weekend, loud week: CPI Tuesday, orders stay put
brief.market_summary: Markets are closed for the weekend, so Friday's closes still stand. The S&P 500 is at 7,376.86 after −2.7% on the week, its worst since June. The Nasdaq is in a correction, and the VIX is 25.64. Treasuries have rallied over the month, with the 10Y at 4.859% (−37bp), even though December hike odds rose to about 75–80% after October payrolls came in at 165k. Friday itself was a bear flattener: 2Y +5bp, 30Y +1bp. Brent settled at $98.32 after a weekly fall of roughly 13–17% on hopes of a US–Iran deal and restored Gulf exports. Crypto trades through the weekend but has gone nowhere: BTC is $75,946, about $1K above the ~$75K level traders call the breakdown, after $1.28B of spot ETF outflows last week.
brief.since_last: Not much has changed. The only new prices are weekend crypto quotes, and they are flat: BTC +0.28%, ETH +0.07%, SOL −0.06%, TON −2.4%. No US data came out on Saturday. Berkshire reported Q3 on Saturday: operating earnings $12.71B (−6% y/y), about $9.6B of Q3 buybacks plus about $2B more in October, and GEICO earnings down about 45%. The stock reacts Monday. New headlines: Democrats say ending Trump's tariffs is a top priority (n18); Iran escalation risk is still described as high despite the deal talk (n127); Fed Chair Warsh spoke on AI and rates (n55); S&P 500 earnings are beating estimates by the narrowest margin in about four years (n23). Several headlines look stale or mis-dated, so don't trade on them. n85 ("Hot CPI Inflation Seals Fed Rate Hike") cannot be about October, because October CPI is only due Tuesday. n82 ("Dow Soars 500") contradicts Friday's Dow −0.46%. n42 describes Thursday's rout. n90's Diwali item is about Indian markets; the session calendar shows the next regular US session as Monday 09:30 ET. Sources disagree on a few figures: Brent's weekly drop (13.2% vs 16–17%, depending on how the contract roll is treated) and Fed speaker times. The crypto snapshot timestamp also doesn't line up neatly with the brief time.

economic_data.takeaway: October still carries high energy prices: by the snapshot's 1M and 1W changes, Brent traded around $104–118 during the month. A hot headline would therefore look backward, because oil has since fallen 16%. A headline at 0.5% or more would still push 2Y yields and the dollar higher and hit tech, since hike odds are already about 75–80%.

This is the number that decides the week. At 0.2% or below, the December hike looks like a one-off and tech probably gets a relief rally. At 0.4% or above, a series of hikes gets priced, the front end sells off, and the 10Y auction at 13:00 the same day could tail.
Claims below 200K back up Friday's strong payrolls and keep the hike priced. Only a jump well above 220K would change the Fed narrative.
September's 1.3% was oil-driven. A large drop is expected and would confirm the pipeline is cooling. A print near 1% would undercut the idea that the inflation scare is fading along with oil.
Another 0.7% would suggest energy costs are leaking into margins and services. That is bad for duration and for richly valued equities.

earnings.result: Q3 operating earnings $12.71B (−6% y/y), net $22.11B (−28%), revenue $105.65B (+11%). GEICO earnings were down about 45%; rail, energy and manufacturing were up. Buybacks were about $9.6B in Q3 (more than double Q2) plus about $2B in October. No consensus figure was found.
earnings.takeaway: Management is buying back stock aggressively in a falling market, which signals they see Berkshire's own value as cheap. The insurance weakness is the soft spot. Expect a modest Monday reaction; it says little about the index.
This is a direct read on AI power demand after Thursday's political scare over data-centre construction. Weak contract commentary would extend the selloff from chips into power.
Listen for anything about private credit and data-centre financing. The AI selloff is moving into credit (n130), and KKR's tone will show whether that is a funding problem or just a valuation one.

The Q3 numbers reflect higher oil and should look good. What matters is guidance at $90 WTI after XLE fell 12% on the week. Capex or buyback cuts would confirm energy equities are re-rating to lower oil.

CoreWeave is the poster child for debt-funded AI capacity, the group that sold off first (n101). Its backlog and financing commentary land the same night as CPI and will set the tone for SMH and XLK into AMAT.

earnings.result: Est EPS $4.06 vs $2.17 last year, a high bar that roughly doubles.
earnings.takeaway: This is the cleanest read on whether chipmakers are cutting equipment orders after the AI-capex scare. A strong guide could squeeze SMH back toward pre-Thursday levels; a soft one validates the trim.
AI networking orders are the swing factor. As the largest reporter this week ($377B), it moves XLK directly.

sections.summary: Nothing has traded since Friday. The S&P 500 is at 7,376.86 after its worst week since June. Thursday's drop of more than 4%, the worst day since April 2025, was driven by fear that a Democratic Congress slows AI data-centre building. Friday's chip bounce (SMH +3.6%) didn't undo the damage, and the weekend headlines add more reasons for caution: the narrowest earnings beats in about four years (n23), record margin debt (n57), and stocks falling together (n41, n63).
key_points: Week: S&P −2.7%, Nasdaq −3.4% (in correction), Russell −2.1%, Dow −0.9%. XLK −8.2% on the week and −16.7% on the month; SMH −23.6% on the month.
Rotation is clear over the month: XLV +9.9%, XLP +8.0%, XLF +5.4%, XLY +5.3%, XLU +5.0%. Dow flat (+0.1%).
VIX is 25.64 (−9% Friday but +66% on the month), so daily swings of about 2% are normal right now.
Democrats aim to end tariffs (n18), which is a possible support for importers and goods inflation. It is a policy path, not an event this week.

sections.summary: The long end is pricing slower growth while the front end prices a December hike. The 10Y is at 4.859%, down 37bp on the month, and the 2Y is at 4.51%, with 2s10s at +35bp. Friday's jobs beat produced a bear flattener (2Y +5bp, 10Y +2bp, 30Y +1bp). This week brings $125B of coupon supply wrapped around CPI. Credit is lagging Treasuries, so the AI stress is reaching corporate bonds.
key_points: December hike odds are about 75–80% (CME and LSEG) after payrolls of 165k and wages +0.4% m/m.
Supply: 3Y $58B on Monday, 10Y $42B on Tuesday at 13:00 (4.5 hours after CPI), 30Y $25B on Thursday. Wednesday is Veterans Day, and the cash bond market is likely closed (check SIFMA).
Over the month, LQD is +2.0% but HYG only +0.1%. Data-centre borrowers sold off first (n101, n130).
The 3M bill is about 4.19% (par), so SGOV still pays well while you wait for entry levels.

sections.summary: Brent settled at $98.32 after roughly a 13–17% weekly drop, the biggest since 2020 or 2022 depending on how the contract roll is counted. Three things drove it: US–Iran talks showing progress (including a floated 48-hour Hormuz reopening via Qatar), Saudi and UAE exports back to prewar levels, and a firmer dollar. Tanker attacks and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries are what's stopping the fall, and CNBC still describes escalation risk as high (n127). Prices are stale until Sunday evening ET.
key_points: Brent is −16.4% on the week and −5.7% on the month; WTI is $90.83. The dollar index rose 0.72% Friday to 102.28.
EIA crude fell 865k barrels against an expected +877k build, a mildly bullish surprise that got overwhelmed.
OPEC+ held its December targets (third straight pause); the ministerial meeting is 29 Nov. Iraq is pushing for a higher quota (n103). Saxo sees support at $70–90 as inventories rebuild (n75).

Catalysts: OXY on Monday after the close, the EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook on Tuesday, the OPEC monthly report on Wednesday, and any Iran headline at any hour. n98 ('extend gains') and n111 ('below $95') conflict with Friday's flat settle; treat both as stale or intraday.

Holders of the US-listed spot ETFs are the steady sellers: −$1.28B from BTC ETFs on the week, which turns 2026 year-to-date flows negative, and a sixth straight week of ETH ETF outflows. Over one month: BTC −8.4%, ETH −10.1%, SOL −18.6% (lowest since 22 Aug), XRP −16.5%, ADA −24%, TON −28.6%.
Saylor hints at another Strategy buy with 849K BTC held (n29, n39). Hayes warns of near-term pressure (n25). Liquidations have been small (−$16M, n64).
Negatives specific to individual chains: the PBOC halted a Solana event in Shanghai (n66), Binance France is closing accounts on 31 Dec (n54), and ETH's Glamsterdam testnet is delayed.

brief.instructor_take: Only crypto traded this weekend, and it barely moved. So today is for preparing orders, not acting. The week is packed. Tuesday has CPI at 08:30, a $42B 10-year auction at 13:00 and CoreWeave after the close. Wednesday is probably a bond-market holiday. Thursday brings a $25B 30-year auction plus AMAT and Cisco, and PPI comes Friday. Here's what I'd want you to notice. October CPI covers a month when Brent traded roughly $104–118, so a hot headline is old news now that oil is $98. Core CPI is the real decider: 0.2% expected vs 0.3% prior, and it tells us whether the December hike, already about 75–80% priced, becomes the first of several. I think the crowd is too quick to call Friday's chip bounce the bottom. Earnings beats are the thinnest in about four years, margin debt is at a record $1.502T, and the AI selloff is reaching credit: HYG is flat on the month while LQD is up 2%. So I've set orders that each do something useful whichever way CPI lands. A soft print lifts tech into my XLK sell limits. A hot print plus a weak auction pushes the 10Y toward 4.95–5.05%, where my IEF bids sit. I'm staying out of Brent and crypto this week. Oil swings both ways on Iran headlines, and BTC has ETF holders selling every day. What would change my mind: core CPI at 0.2% or lower together with a strong AMAT guide. Then I'd judge the rotation out of tech done for now and stop trimming.

top_ideas.title: Trim tech overweight into a CPI/AMAT bounce
top_ideas.one_liner: Keep XLK sell limits at $166.50/$169 into CPI and AMAT
top_ideas.thesis: Tech has fallen 16.7% in a month, but none of the causes has gone away: hike odds of about 75–80%, political risk to AI capex, credit stress at data-centre borrowers, and thin earnings beats. Use the volatility this week's catalysts will bring to sell a third of the overweight at higher prices rather than into the hole.
top_ideas.reasoning: XLK closed Friday at $164.74, 1.1% below my first limit and 2.6% below my second. With the VIX at 25.64, one good day after a soft CPI or a strong AMAT can fill both, so I keep the orders rather than chase. The principle is that I size the position for the current conditions rather than react to price: in a Fed-hiking market, a concentrated AI-capex bet is more risk than a moderate investor should carry. Debt-funded data-centre names sold first (n101), and the stress is spreading into credit (n130), which tells me the selloff is about financing and politics, not one bad quarter. I use XLK because that's where the overweight sits; if your concentration is in semis, put matching limits on SMH, which has the bigger beta. A less experienced investor sees −17% and either panic-sells or buys the dip; the better move is to let a bounce come to you. I'd stop trimming if XLK closes above $177, because a recovery like that alongside a 0.2% core CPI would mean the market has absorbed the scare. I'm uncertain on one point: Friday's 3.6% SMH rebound could be the start of a real recovery. That's why I'm trimming a third, not exiting.

top_ideas.title: Buy 7–10Y Treasuries on a CPI/auction back-up
top_ideas.one_liner: Bid IEF at $91.20/$90.60 for a CPI or auction back-up
top_ideas.thesis: The 10Y has fallen 37bp in a month even as hike odds rose, which says the long end expects hikes to slow growth and oil's collapse to cool inflation. Tuesday has CPI and a $42B 10-year auction within hours of each other, and Thursday has the 30-year. That gives good odds of a temporary back-up toward 4.95–5.05%, a better entry than today's 4.86%.
top_ideas.reasoning: I don't want to buy IEF at $91.86 after a 37bp rally and just ahead of CPI, because I'd have no edge there. My limits work out, using IEF's roughly 7-year duration, to about a 4.96% 10Y at $91.20 and about 5.05% at $90.60. A hot core CPI followed by a weak auction that afternoon is exactly what could get us there. Friday's bear flattener is the evidence the long end is anchored: the 2Y rose 5bp on a big jobs beat while the 30Y moved 1bp. I prefer IEF to TLT because the 30Y at 5.26% carries more of the term-premium and fiscal risk, with only $25B of Thursday supply to absorb. A beginner might also assume a Fed hike is bad for every bond; in practice hikes often help the 7–10Y sector by lowering future inflation. I cancel if the 10Y trades below 4.75% before filling, because the trade will have left without me. I'm wrong if the 10Y closes above 5.20% (IEF about $89.6), or if Waller or Williams signal a series of hikes rather than one. Don't add or change orders on Wednesday: Veterans Day likely closes the cash bond market, and IEF spreads can widen.

top_ideas.title: Health care: finish the add only at $184 or lower
top_ideas.one_liner: Finish the XLV add at $183.50; never pay above $184
top_ideas.thesis: Health care is where money has gone during the AI-capex and rate scare (XLV +9.9% in a month). It held flat on Friday's tech bounce and through Humana's results. I'll complete the position only on a small dip, because the sector has already re-rated.
top_ideas.reasoning: XLV closed Friday at $184.80, down 0.06% on the day and flat on the week. That tells me two things: the tech bounce didn't pull money back out, and Humana's Friday report did no visible damage, although I found no beat or miss details. The logic is a defensive rotation: health care earnings depend little on AI capex or on the hike path. That makes it a sensible home for money coming out of tech, especially if Tuesday's CPI is hot. The trap a less experienced investor falls into is chasing a sector after a 10% month. So I insist on $183.50, and if it doesn't fill, I'm fine owning half. I chose XLV over XLP because staples fell 1.28% Friday and are more sensitive to rates and input costs. My conviction is low because a soft CPI could reverse the rotation quickly. A Democratic Congress also adds drug-pricing headline risk, which the market hasn't tested yet. A close below $176 or a guidance cut from Humana, Cigna or Novo would tell me the defensive case is broken.

lesson.explanation: A bear flattener is when yields rise (bonds fall, hence 'bear') and short maturities rise more than long ones, so the gap between them narrows. It usually happens when the market prices more Fed tightening. Short-dated bonds track the policy rate directly. Long-dated bonds are partly anchored by the expectation that hikes will slow growth and inflation later. Seeing it tells you the market believes the Fed and doubts the economy can take many hikes.
lesson.todays_example: Friday's 165k payrolls pushed December hike odds to about 75–80%. The 2Y rose 5bp to 4.51%, the 10Y 2bp to 4.86% and the 30Y only 1bp to 5.26%, and 2s10s narrowed to +35bp. That is why I'm buying the 7–10Y sector (IEF) rather than the 1–3Y sector (SHY), and only on a back-up: further hikes mainly reprice short yields.
